# Fall River/New Bedford Line

## Overview

The Fall River/New Bedford Line, commonly referred to as part of the South Coast Rail project, is a commuter rail service extension in southeastern Massachusetts intended to connect the cities of Fall River and New Bedford to Boston via the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) network. The initiative represents a significant state transportation development, focused on enhancing mobility, fostering economic growth, and providing improved transit options for communities historically underserved by direct rail access to Boston. The South Coast Rail project, which includes the Fall River and New Bedford branches, has been one of the largest and most anticipated public transportation efforts in Massachusetts, involving extensive state and federal coordination, environmental review, and public engagement. Service on the line was scheduled to begin upon completion of construction, with the projected opening factoring in decades of study, planning, and phased implementation.

## History

### Early Proposals and Rationale

Efforts to reconnect southeastern Massachusetts (specifically, Fall River and New Bedford) with Boston by rail date to the late 20th century, following decades without direct commuter service after the original lines ceased passenger operations in the mid-20th century. The stated goals of restoration included reducing roadway congestion, improving regional equity in transportation, and supporting economic development in the South Coast region, which had higher unemployment and slower job growth relative to other parts of the state.

### Project Development and Delays

The South Coast Rail project has experienced a protracted planning and implementation process. Various environmental, political, and fiscal challenges led to repeated delays over several decades. Original service targets were set for the early 2000s, but shifting state priorities, changes in administration, and cost escalations repeatedly delayed construction and opening dates. Substantial progress accelerated in the late 2010s and 2020s due to renewed state commitments, federal funding, and formalization of the project under MassDOT and MBTA authority.

### Funding and Approvals

The project received funding from both state and federal sources. The total budget, as of the late planning stages, was estimated at over $1 billion for phased development. Key milestones included completion of the federal and state environmental review, public comment and hearings, and phased design-build contracts awarded to construction firms. The Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs played a major role in overseeing the Environmental Impact Statement process, addressing issues such as wetlands, wildlife habitats, and neighborhood impacts.

## Route Description

The Fall River/New Bedford Line consists of two main branches, both originating near Middleborough and extending south toward the urban centers of Fall River and New Bedford. The line utilizes a combination of existing freight tracks, upgraded infrastructure, and new segments to accommodate commuter rail operations.

- **Northern Connection:** The route connects with Boston’s South Station through the existing MBTA Middleborough/Lakeville Line, leveraging existing rail infrastructure before diverging near Middleborough to serve the new South Coast corridor.
- **Branch Alignment:** After the shared section, the route splits into two branches—one serving Fall River and the other serving New Bedford, with intermediate stops in towns such as Freetown, Taunton, and East Taunton.
- **Stations:** The project includes the construction or reconstruction of stations in key South Coast communities. Station locations include, but are not limited to, Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Fall River Depot, and New Bedford.

## Operations

### Operator and Rolling Stock

The MBTA is the designated operator for the South Coast Rail service, including the Fall River/New Bedford Line. Operations are planned to use standard MBTA commuter rail rolling stock, consistent with other lines in the regional system. Maintenance and layover facilities have been incorporated into the project’s design.

### Service Pattern

Scheduled service is designed to connect the South Coast communities to Boston, with peak and off-peak operations to accommodate both commuters and non-commuters. The projected schedule provides direct access to Boston’s South Station, and service frequency, travel times, and fares are established in accordance with MBTA policies and system norms.

## Infrastructure

### Track and Signaling

The project encompasses the reconstruction of existing tracks, new sidings, modern signaling, and grade crossing improvements. Upgrades are necessary to support faster, more frequent, and higher-capacity commuter rail trains, as opposed to previous freight-only service. Accessibility features for passengers with disabilities are integrated at all new and reconstructed stations, in compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).

### Environmental Considerations

Significant portions of the project required mitigation measures to address environmental impacts, notably in sensitive wetland areas and near wildlife habitats. The Environmental Impact Report (EIR) and public review led to modifications in design and construction methodology to reduce negative effects and meet regulatory requirements.

## Service Milestones

- **Project Launch:** After decades of feasibility studies, the reconstructed line’s construction began in earnest in the late 2010s.
- **Phased Implementation:** The project adopted a phased approach, with an initial "Early Service" alternative via Middleborough prioritized to expedite the resumption of service while work continued on a longer-term, full-build alignment.
- **Scheduled Opening:** The timeline for the initial phase projected the commencement of service in the mid-2020s, following completion of necessary track, station, and systems upgrades. Updated projections and opening ceremonies are publicized on the MassDOT and MBTA project pages.

## Controversies and Notable Events

### Delays and Political Debates

The South Coast Rail project—including the Fall River/New Bedford Line—has been the subject of recurring delays linked to changing state administrations, shifting budget priorities, and the complexity of the planning process. Timelines often slipped by several years as project scope and estimated costs evolved.

### Environmental Review and Community Response

The environmental review process, involving both state and federal agencies, generated significant public comment. Some environmental advocates and local residents voiced concerns about potential impacts on wetlands, river crossings, and local ecosystems. The requirement for special permits and mitigation led to design changes and additional costs.

### Contracting and Procurement Issues

The competitive bidding process for construction contracts generated some disputes, including protests over bid awards and debate regarding labor agreements. MassDOT and the MBTA addressed these through formal procurement review procedures.

### Community and Public Meetings

The planning process included extensive public outreach, with numerous town hall sessions and open houses. Supporters emphasized the potential economic and quality-of-life benefits for the South Coast, while opponents sometimes expressed apprehension about neighborhood disruption, cost, and project scope.

## Future Plans

Post-opening, the South Coast Rail project plans further infrastructure upgrades and expanded service options. The "Full Build" alternative, with a direct link through Stoughton, has been retained as a long-term goal, pending additional funding and resolution of further environmental and engineering considerations. MBTA and MassDOT will continue to evaluate service levels and infrastructure needs in response to ridership and operational feedback.

Connecting Boston and Southeastern Massachusetts

The South Coast Rail project will restore commuter rail service between Boston and southeastern Massachusetts. ![Image 1: Two trains pulled into the platforms at East Taunton Commuter Rail station](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2025-04/2025-03-24-south-coast-rail-east-taunton-opening.jpg?itok=BPrgcX6B)

The East Taunton station platform on the first day of Fall River/New Bedford Line service (March 24, 2025)

About This Project
------------------

![Image 2: Newly renovated New Bedford station with station sign and platform with yellow tactile surface indicator ](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2024-06/2024-04-SCR-New-Bedford-Renovated-Station-Platform.jpg?itok=F511KnUe)

New Bedford station platform (April 2024)

The [South Coast Rail project](https://www.mass.gov/south-coast-rail) offers a reliable transit connection between southeastern Massachusetts and Boston. Riders can take a one-seat trip for the first time since the late 1950s.

The project creates connections between Boston and the communities of Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River, the only three major cities within 50 miles of Boston that previously didn’t have Commuter Rail access.

[Learn more about the South Coast Rail Program](https://www.mass.gov/service-details/about-the-south-coast-rail-project)

Building a Better T
-------------------

As part of our $9.6 billion, [5-year capital investment plan](https://www.mbta.com/cip), we're renovating stations, modernizing fare collection systems, upgrading services for our buses, subways, and ferries, and improving the accessibility of the entire system.

[Learn more](https://www.mbta.com/projects)

Schedules
---------

On weekdays, trains run every 70 minutes. There are 32 direct trips to or from [South Station](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-sstat) including:

*   15 trips between South Station and Fall River
*   17 trips between South Station and New Bedford

On weekends, there are 26 total trips with trains running every two hours.

[View the Fall River/New Bedford Line schedule](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable)

[Check alerts for the Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/alerts)

### Scheduled Transfers at East Taunton Station

In addition to the 32 direct trips to or from South Station on weekdays, we operate connecting trains between:

*   Fall River Depot and East Taunton station
*   New Bedford station and East Taunton station

Riders can transfer between connecting trains and direct trains at East Taunton station where the Fall River and New Bedford branches meet. This means riders on both branches can access more trips to or from South Station throughout the weekday.

For example, riders going between New Bedford and South Station can get to their destination even if the next direct trip is between Fall River and South Station:

1.  At New Bedford station, board the connecting train going to East Taunton station.
2.  At East Taunton station, exit the connecting train to make a transfer.
3.  Board the direct train that came from Fall River Depot and is continuing to South Station.

1.  At South Station, board the direct train going to Fall River Depot.
2.  At East Taunton station, exit the direct train to make a transfer.
3.  Board the connecting train going to New Bedford station.

We've coordinated train schedules to ensure that riders always have enough time to transfer at East Taunton.

* * *

Safety First Program
--------------------

**Safety First** is a program that educates people on how to stay safe around train tracks. Our goal is to bring an understanding of safety rules to all residents in every southeastern Massachusetts city and town.

Through presentations, brochures, videos, meetings, and conversations, you’ll learn safety basics. You can watch and share our [Safety Video Series](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLpgUaADAtNfuJKpPGysCprwkepiOC-DBZ) developed for children, teens, and the general public to learn about the importance of safety for everyone throughout the region.

Watch our safety videos, and please think **Safety First**.

To request rail safety education or materials, call Customer Support at [617-222-3200](tel:617-222-3200) or fill out our [Customer Support form](https://www.mbta.com/customer-support).

[Download a Safety First fact sheet](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2023-12-safety-first-fact-sheet.pdf) (PDF, 926 KB)

[### Commuter Rail Safety](https://www.mbta.com/safety/commuter-rail-safety)![Image 3: Bi-level Commuter Rail coaches at the newly-completed Freetown Station](https://live-mbta.pantheonsite.io/sites/default/files/styles/teaser/public/media/2023-03/2023-3-3-cr-scr-freetown-ribbon-cutting-double-car-view.jpg?itok=9iFomq_d)

Commuter Rail safety is important to the MBTA. We aim to educate our riders and community members about Commuter Rail safety to prevent any accidents or close calls.

[Learn more](https://www.mbta.com/safety/commuter-rail-safety)

Construction Timeline
---------------------

South Coast Rail is being built in phases:

*   **Phase 1:** Extended the former Middleborough/Lakeville Line, now named the Fall River/New Bedford Line. Service on the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable) started March 24, 2025.
*   **Full Build:** Extends the Stoughton Line south to connect more communities to the Fall River/New Bedford Line.

Phase 1 broke ground in July 2019, with major construction beginning in 2020. After we completed construction of stations, tracks, and signals, we also conducted rigorous testing to meet safety certifications and qualifications that precede passenger service.

Construction was divided into two contracts, with early action work preceding both:

*   Construction of the Fall River Secondary Line, which will connect Fall River to Boston
*   Construction of the New Bedford Main Line, the Middleborough Secondary Line, and the signal system for the entire Phase 1 corridor, which will connect Taunton, New Bedford, and Fall River to Boston

[See a map of the Phase 1 corridor](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2024-12-18-south-coast-rail-phase-1-corridor-map-updated.pdf) (PDF, 9.1 MB)

![Image 4: A crew works on culvert installation in Lakeville as part of the South Coast Rail project (May 2020)](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2020-05/SCR_Culvert_Installation2020.jpg?itok=7KdZdwqv)

A crew replaces rail above a completed culvert installation in Lakeville as part of the South Coast Rail project (May 2020)

Our crews completed early action work in fall 2020 in preparation for Phase 1 construction:

*   Replaced four railroad bridges
*   Installed 46 culverts as part of the drainage system
*   Ordered and stored long-lead special track materials in advance to reduce construction delays
*   Constructed five wetland mitigation areas and began monitoring their success

[Learn more about early action work](https://www.mass.gov/lists/south-coast-rail-documents-and-meeting-materials#spring-2019-fact-sheet-)

![Image 5: 16 bi-level coaches, like the one pictured here, will be put into service as part of the South Coast Rail project ](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2020-05/SCR_Bi-levelCoach.jpg?itok=-3Jgz3cU)

16 bi-level coaches, like the one pictured here, will be put into service during Phase 1 of the South Coast Rail project

In October 2019, the Fiscal and Management Control Board (FMCB) [approved the purchase of 16 bi-level coaches](https://www.mbta.com/news/2019-09-23/fmcb-approves-the-procurement-80-new-commuter-rail-bi-level-coaches) to meet the needs of the South Coast Rail project. The refurbishment of two locomotives required for South Coast Rail service is also complete. As of summer 2023, these vehicles are part of the state's commuter rail system inventory.

*   ![Image 6: Newly completed Freetown Station platform](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2023-03/2023-3-3-cr-scr-freetown-ribbon-cutting-platform-view.jpg?itok=rACkugcF)
    
    The Completed Freetown Station during the ribbon-cutting event celebrating the substantial completion of the Fall River Secondary Line contract (December 2022)
    
*   The Fall River Secondary Line extends to Fall River through Freetown and Taunton, providing direct service between Fall River and Boston. This new Commuter Rail line includes two stations in Freetown and Fall River, and a layover facility at Weaver’s Cove in Fall River. We completed construction at the end of 2024.

**Completed Work**

Crews reconstructed 12.1 miles of the Fall River Secondary Line, which was previously a freight line, to lift speed restrictions and allow for Commuter Rail service. Work also included tree clearing, erosion control, and survey work along the tracks. The tracks were reconstructed, resulting in improved freight service in the region.

Construction included the following:

*   Nine rail bridges
*   10 new grade crossings and four interlockings
*   Two new stations and a layover facility for storing trains overnight

Trains on the completed Fall River Secondary Line travel through Berkley, Freetown, and Fall River.

[See a map of the Fall River Secondary Line](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_FRS_Map.pdf)

![Image 7: view of rail layover yard with blue sky](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_650x650/public/media/2025-01/2024-09-10-scr-wamsutta-layover-yard.jpeg?itok=BrdJ5T4o)

Wamsutta layover yard (September 2024)

The Middleborough Secondary Line extends from Middleborough through Taunton and into New Bedford to provide direct service between New Bedford and Boston.

The new Commuter Rail line includes four stations and a layover facility adjacent to the existing one in Wamsutta.

We completed construction for the Middleborough Secondary and New Bedford Main lines in fall 2024. We completed construction for the pedestrian bridge at [New Bedford](https://www.mbta.com/stops/place-NBM-0546) station in spring 2025.

**Completed Work**

Crews reconstructed 24.1 miles of Middleborough Secondary and the New Bedford Main lines, which are currently active freight lines, to lift speed restrictions and allow for Commuter Rail service. The right-of-way (ROW) was also reconstructed, resulting in improved freight service in the region.

Construction included:

*   Six rail bridges, constructed to meet state-of-good-repair guidelines
*   18 grade crossings and 14 interlockings
*   Four new stations and a layover facility for storing trains overnight
*   Signal systems and [positive train control (PTC)](https://www.mbta.com/projects/commuter-rail-positive-train-control-ptc) for the entire Phase 1 corridor

Work took place in Middleborough, Taunton, Lakeville, Freetown, and New Bedford. Testing for the entire South Coast Rail occurred under this contract.

Work has been completed on the Fall River Secondary Line to overlay signals and communications.

[See a map of the Middleborough Secondary and New Bedford lines](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/2020-05/SCR_MSNBML_map.pdf)

[Read the press release](https://www.mbta.com/news/2020-08-24/fmcb-approves-4035-million-contract-south-coast-rail-main-line-construction)

The Full Build will extend Commuter Rail service on the Stoughton Main Line and Northeast Corridor (north of Canton Junction). It will bring service to Taunton and connect more communities in the region.

This stage presents more challenges related to wetland impacts, complex engineering, electrification, and cost. The next steps include starting conceptual design work, preliminary engineering, and securing funding.
